note: `mypy nestor` failed in any dev environment with .[semantic] resolved. fastembed pulls numpy, whose stubs use 3.12+ `type` statements and are a syntax error under the 3.10 python_version pin; one error in numpy's own .pyi aborts the run before nestor is checked at all. So scripts/ci-lint.sh went red locally while CI -- which installs the five lint tools only, no package and no extras -- stayed green. The agent that hit this had just installed .[dev] to fix a different gap, which is the ordinary way to arrive here.

decisions.question: A local extra makes a gate fail that CI passes. Which side is wrong?
decisions.commitment: Neither verdict is wrong; the gate is, for letting the environment decide. ignore_missing_imports only speaks to the absent case, so an installed extra sends mypy into that dependency's own stubs. follow_imports = "skip" on the same override block makes the four optional integrations Any whether installed or not, so local and CI agree by construction rather than by everyone's venv matching the lint job's. Verified in both environments -- local venv with extras present, and a CI-shaped venv with lint tools only -- each reporting no issues in the same 41 source files, so coverage did not shrink.
decisions.why: This is agent-log §6.110 in the mirror. There a local .[keys] env resolved an import and hid a gap until keys-absent CI turned red; here a local extra breaks a gate CI passes. Both are one defect -- the verdict moving with which extras happen to be installed -- and the block's own comment already stated the principle: this gate checks nestor's own code.

decisions.question: Raising python_version to 3.12 would also have made it pass. Why not?
decisions.commitment: 3.10 is the requires-python floor and the low row of the test matrix, so the pin is what makes the gate catch code that would break on the oldest Python still supported. It stays. Trading that for silence about a dependency nestor does not carry would be paying a real check to settle a false alarm.
decisions.why: The failure was in numpy's stubs, not in nestor. Changing what the gate checks in order to stop it reporting on something it should not have been reading is the shape of a gate quietly narrowing -- the same move the _is_secret_path note in 0157 refuses for the same reason.

decisions.question: How do we know the gate still bites after being told to skip imports?
decisions.commitment: By making it fail on purpose: an `int` returned as `str` was injected into nestor/triage, and mypy flagged it at nestor/triage/__init__.py:157 and exited 1. Then reverted. The file count before and after is identical (41), so nothing dropped out of coverage silently.
decisions.why: An override that makes a red gate go green has two explanations and they look the same from the outside. Proving it still refuses a real error is the only way to tell "we stopped reading someone else's stubs" from "we stopped reading".
